n: Spot it: Only long bone that lies horizontally in anatomical position; a strut connecting the scapula to the sternum.
Spot it: Flat bone on the back of the upper trunk. Orient: view from behind with the spine visible and the glenoid cavity lateral.
Spot it: The axillary border is the thickest border of the scapula.
Spot it: The coracoid process is an attachment site for some shoulder and arm muscles.
Spot it: The glenoid cavity is where the scapula articulates with the head of the humerus.
Spot it: The scapular notch allows room for the suprascapular nerve to pass over the scapula.
Spot it: This is the anterior surface of the scapula and is the surface sliding on the ribs and trunk.
Spot it: The edge running horizontally along the top of the triangular scapula.
Spot it: This is the edge of the scapula that is closest to the vertebrae.
Spot it: Orient: trochlea medial to capitulum, olecranon fossa posterior (out of view) = anterior view; the rounded head points to the glenoid cavity.
Spot it: The capitulum is the site where the humerus articulates with the radius.
Spot it: Coronoid means shaped like a crow’s beak.
Spot it: The deltoid tuberosity is the attachment site for the deltoid muscle.
Spot it: The greater tubercle is a site for muscles attachment.
Spot it: The head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula.
Spot it: The lesser tubercle is a site for muscle attachment.
Spot it: The radial fossa allows room for the bones of the forearm to move when the arm is bent.
Spot it: The trochlea is the site where the humerus articulates with the ulna.
Spot it: Lateral forearm bone (thumb side) in anatomical position; rotates around the ulna.
Spot it: The head of the radius articulates with the capitulum of the humerus.
Spot it: The radial neck is the constricted shaft of the radius just distal to the flared head of the radius.
Spot it: The radial tuberosity is an attachment point for the biceps brachii muscle.
Spot it: The ulnar notch is where the radius articulates with the head of the ulna.
Spot it: Medial forearm bone (pinky side); the "elbow bone".
Spot it: Coronoid means shaped like the beak of a crow.
Spot it: The head of the ulna articulates with the radius (at the ulnar notch of the radius).
Spot it: The olecranon process of the ulna is the point of the elbow.
Spot it: The radial notch is where the radius rotates around the ulna.
Spot it: The trochlear or semilunar notch fits over the trochlea of the humerus.
Spot it: The ulnar tuberosity is the attachment site of a ligament that joins the ulna and radius.
Spot it: The scaphoid is so named because it is boat shaped.
Spot it: The lunate is so named because it is moon shaped.
Spot it: The triquetrum or triquetral is so named because it has three corners.
Spot it: The pisiform is so named because it is pea shaped.
Spot it: The trapezium is so named because it is shaped like a geometric figure called a trapezium.
Spot it: The trapezoid is so named because it is shaped like a geometric figure called a trapezoid.
Spot it: The capitate is so named because it is head shaped.
Spot it: The hamate is so named because it has a hooked process on the palmar side.
Spot it: Five bones of the palm; always refer to them by number (1 = thumb side, 5 = pinky side).
Spot it: long slender bone between base of index finger and wrist.
Spot it: long slender bone between base of middle finger and wrist.
Spot it: long slender bone between base of ring finiger and wrist.
Spot it: long slender bone between base of pinky finger and wrist.
Spot it: Digit bones: fingers have proximal, middle and distal phalanges; the thumb has only proximal and distal.
Spot it: Tip of the finger, under the fingernail.
Spot it: Small bone between the most distal knuckle and the middle knuckle. The thumb has no middle phalanx.
Spot it: Small bone between the most proximal knuckle and the middle knuckle.
Spot it: Three regions: manubrium, body and xiphoid process.
Spot it: This is the middle and most large portion of the sternum.
Spot it: The clavicular notch is where the clavicle joins with the sternum.
Spot it: This is the broad section of the top part of the sternum. It is kind of square shaped.
Spot it: The sternal angle is the point where the manubrium joins the body of the sternum.
Spot it: The word xiphoid comes from a Greek word that means sword shaped.
Spot it: 24 ribs (12 pairs): 7 pairs true, 5 pairs false (the last 2 of them floating).
Spot it: The head of each rib is where it attaches to the vertebrae.
Spot it: The neck is between the head and tubercle of the rib.
Spot it: The tubercle of the rib articulates with the transverse process of the thoracic vertebrae.
Spot it: The angle of the rib is just lateral to the tubercle and is the area of greatest curvature.
Spot it: The body is the main part of the rib.
Spot it: The costal groove contains vessels and nerves.
Spot it: The costal cartilage is a hyaline cartilage extension of the ribs that attach them to the sternum.
Spot it: The five pairs of the false ribs are so named because they do not attach directly to the sternum.
Spot it: The seven pairs of true ribs are so named because they attach directly with their costal cartilage to the sternum.
Spot it: The body is the weightbearing portion of the vertebra.
Spot it: The inferior intervertebral notch helps make up the intervertebral foramen.
Spot it: Each intervertebral foramen is an opening through which spinal nerves exit the spinal cord.
Spot it: The lamina is part of the vertebral arch.
Spot it: The pedicle is part of the vertebral arch and attaches it to the body of the vertebrae.
Spot it: The superior intervertebral notch helps make up the intervertebral foramen.
Spot it: The vertebral arch projects posteriorly from the body.
Spot it: The vertebral foramen of adjacent vertebrae combine to form the vertebral canal for the spinal cord.
Spot it: 7 vertebrae; atlas (C1) and axis (C2) are unique; only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina.
Spot it: The atlas is the first cervical vertebrae.
Spot it: The axis is the second cervical vertebrae.
Spot it: The bifid spinous processes of many of the cervical vertebrae are so named because they are split in two.
Spot it: Both dens and odontoid mean “tooth shaped.”
Spot it: Only cervical vertebrae have a transverse foramen.
Spot it: 12 vertebrae; costal facets for the ribs.
Spot it: The costal facet is where the tubercle of each rib articulates with the thoracic vertebrae.
Spot it: 5 vertebrae; the largest bodies of all vertebrae, short thick spinous process.
Spot it: Large triangle formed by 5 fused vertebrae; links the spine to the pelvis.
Spot it: The auricular surface is where the sacrum joins to the pelvic bones.
Spot it: The sacral canal holds the sacral nerves that have descended from the spinal cord.
Spot it: Formed by the fusion of 3-5 vertebrae; attachment point for several muscles.
